messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur, a 69-year-old financial analyst, had been widowed for three years when the memory of his wife’s final hours finally drove him into a therapist’s office. It happened on a Tuesday: he was alone in his home office, reviewing quarterly earnings reports, when the image of her face—pale, oxygen mask askew—slammed into his mind with the force of a physical blow. His chest tightened, his hands trembled, and a wave of rage surged so abruptly that he slammed his fist onto the desk, cracking the calculator. The anger frightened him more than the memory itself. For months he had told himself he was fine, that grief was for other people. But the intrusions were coming faster now, and the price of keeping them at bay was becoming impossible to ignore.

The traumatic event itself had been neither sudden nor violent. Eleanor’s cancer had been diagnosed late, and the last six weeks were a slow, sterile slide into silence. Arthur had sat beside her hospital bed every evening after work, holding her hand, watching the numbers on the monitors dwindle. What haunted him most was not the moment she stopped breathing—he had looked away, and the nurse had touched his shoulder—but the weeks afterward. At Eleanor’s funeral, surrounded by murmured condolences and wilting lilies, he had felt nothing. An icy distance had taken hold, and he had decided, without quite deciding, that he would not let himself fall apart. He returned to his desk three days later, and no one at the firm asked how he was doing. That suited him fine.

But the numbness came with a price. At work, a colleague’s casual mention of a widowed aunt—a loss theme, he now recognized—sent a spike of heat through his chest. His jaw clenched, and he snapped, “Can we focus on the spreadsheet?” The colleague looked stung, and Arthur said nothing to repair it. He began skipping the weekly team lunch, claiming deadlines. In truth, he was trying to suppress any thought that might lead back to Eleanor—songs on the radio, photographs in drawers, the cemetery where he had not visited since the burial. He told himself it was strength. But the more he pushed the memories away, the more they ambushed him: at the grocery store when he saw her favourite cereal, at a red light when a hearse passed, alone in bed when the silence grew loud.

The causal chains tightened into a self-reinforcing loop. A trigger—say, a news report about a memorial service—would flood him with a mix of guilt and raw fear, his heart racing, his palms slick. That physical threat state, in turn, sharpened his attention to any further loss-related cues; he would scan conversations for dangerous words (“passed,” “miss,” “alone”), and find them everywhere. His habitual emotional numbing, intended to keep him stable, paradoxically amplified the intrusions: by not allowing himself to grieve, he never closed the door on the memory, so it burst through any unguarded moment. Because he never let himself stay with the grief long enough to discover it would not destroy him, his nervous system drew the only conclusion it could — the threat was still live, and any lapse in vigilance could pull him under. And the suppression itself fed his irritability—a short fuse that left him snapping at assistants, muttering under his breath in meetings, and then hating himself for it. Once, after a minor error in a bond calculation, he berated a junior analyst so harshly that the young woman fled to the restroom in tears. Arthur sat at his desk afterward, head in his hands, unable to name what he felt.

After that incident, his supervisor pulled him aside. Softly, she asked if he was okay. He said yes, but the question lodged in his chest like a splinter. That night, for the first time in years, he drove to the cemetery. He sat in the car with the engine running, staring at the headstone from a distance, and felt nothing. Then he felt everything—a cold, shaking terror that he might break apart if he stayed a moment longer. He drove home and, the next morning, called a number a grief pamphlet had given him months ago.

What finally brought Arthur to seek help was not insight but exhaustion. He was tired of bracing for the next memory, tired of the angry outbursts that alienated the few people still willing to be near him, tired of the fortress he had built around his emotions. He told the therapist, in a voice that wavered only slightly, that he was most afraid of one thing: that if he ever let himself truly mourn Eleanor, he would never stop.
